newsitem.title: USA: FOMC voted 12-0 for steady rates at Nov 13 meeting.
newsitem.headline: FOMC voted 12-0 for steady rates at Nov 13 meeting.

text.p: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 12 to zero at its November 13 meeting to keep short-term U.S. interest rates steady and maintained its bias toward tighter credit, according to minutes of the meeting released here on Friday.

The FOMC has met again since its November gathering on Tuesday of this week and it again elected to keep interest rates unchanged. Minutes of that meeting, however, will not be made public until early February.

"While the members expressed varying degrees of concern that tight labor markets and attendant increases in wages might at some point lead to rising price inflation, they agreed there was little or no evidence of such a development at this point and the outlook was far from certain," the minutes said.

This was the fourth consecutive meeting the FOMC elected to have a directive toward tightening. The 5.25-percent federal funds rate and the 5.0-percent discount rate, however, have remained unchanged since February 1.
The minutes also noted "the overall employment cost index in the third quarter, while perhaps understated to some extent, was appreciably below expectations."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan made a reference to the ECI in his July Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress.

The minutes also pointed out that, "with the notable exception of the overall consumer price index, the rate of inflation as measured by various broad price indexes had tended to ease marginally or at worst to stabilize over the past two years."
The minutes also noted FOMC members' "views differed to some extent regarding the most likely course for inflation."

While "several" FOMC members saw the inflation "risks as tilted toward a rise," others felt the "risks surrounding the forecasts for both economic growth and price inflation had become more evenly balanced, but more evidence was needed before a firm judgment could be reached."

The wording of the minutes indicate a lesser degree of concern about the inflation outlook among the FOMC members -- resulting in the absence of a dissent vote and the continuation of a directive toward tightening.
Looking ahead, the FOMC members viewed the "outlook remained subject, as usual, to considerable uncertainty," the minutes said.

"But many of the members observed that underlying trends in key sectors of the economy along with generally supportive financial conditions seemed consistent with further moderate economic expansion," the minutes also said.
Also discussed at the meeting were the level of consumer debt and satisfaction of pent-up demand for big-ticket items that may dampen consumer spending in the future.
Another negative factor cited was "the possibility of a correction in the stock market."
Greenspan earlier this month stirred markets as he questioned whether some U.S. financial assets are overvalued.
